lines.text: Number one on this list was so cruel...
the victim stayed alive for seventeen days.
Seventeen.
Today, seven of the cruelest tortures in history.
Each one worse than the last.
And one of the most famous torture devices of all time...
may have never existed.
Stay until the end, and you'll know which one.
For most of history, torture wasn't a secret.
It was the law.
Courts used it to get confessions.
Kings used it to send a message.
And crowds gathered to watch.
Some of these machines were built by engineers.
Some were invented by tyrants.
All of them were used on real people.
In medieval courts, a confession was called the queen of proofs.
And pain was the fastest way to get one.
Number seven.
The strappado.
It looked simple.
A rope, a pulley, and a beam in the ceiling.
The prisoner's hands were tied behind his back...
and then he was lifted off the ground, by his wrists.
His own weight did the rest.
If he still refused to talk, they tied weights to his feet,
or let him fall, and stopped the rope just before the floor.
The Inquisition loved it, because it left almost no marks.
In fifteen thirteen, one famous man went through it six times...
and confessed nothing.
His name was Niccolò Machiavelli.
Weeks later he was released...
and that same year, he wrote The Prince.
But the strappado was over in minutes.
The next one was designed to make you wait.
Number six.
The rat.
All you needed was a pot, a hungry rat, and fire.
The rat was trapped under a metal pot, on the prisoner's stomach.
Then, they heated the pot with burning coals.
The rat panicked.
And there was only one way out.
It was recorded during the Dutch revolt, in the fifteen hundreds.
And the idea was so terrifying, that George Orwell used it in his novel, 1984,
as the worst fear a human could face.
It needed no dungeon, and no machine.
Just a kitchen pot.
That is what made it so frightening.
Many prisoners confessed... before the coals were even lit.
But some tortures didn't need fire or animals.
Just water.
Number five.
The water drop.
You've probably heard it called Chinese water torture.
But it isn't Chinese.
An Italian lawyer, Hippolytus de Marsiliis, described it five hundred years ago,
after watching drops of water slowly carve a hole in stone.
The prisoner was strapped down, his head locked in place.
And a single cold drop fell on his forehead.
Then another.
At random intervals, so the mind could never relax.
No sleep.
No rest.
Hours became days.
It was said to drive people to madness.
Years ago, a TV experiment put it to the test.
Free to move, it was just annoying.
But strapped down, unable to move...
the volunteer quickly began to panic.
Water breaks the mind.
The next machine... was built to break the body.
Number four.
The rack.
A wooden frame, with a roller at each end.
Ankles tied to one side, wrists to the other.
Every turn of the handle stretched the body a little more.
Until the joints gave way.
The Tower of London kept one.
The guards nicknamed it, the Duke of Exeter's Daughter.
In sixteen oh five, Guy Fawkes, the man who tried to blow up Parliament, was taken there.
King James wrote that the gentler tortures should be used first...
and then, step by step, the worst.
Before, Guy Fawkes signed his name like this.
After the Tower... like this.
And sometimes, they didn't even need to use it.
Prisoners were simply shown the rack...
and that was enough.
But wait.
Before number three, let's talk about the most famous torture device of all.
The iron maiden.
A coffin made of iron, full of spikes.
You've seen it in movies, museums, and video games.
There's just one problem.
There's no real evidence it was ever used.
The famous iron maiden of Nuremberg was put together in the eighteen hundreds, from old pieces,
to impress tourists.
And many of the spiked chairs and masks in torture museums today were made the same way.
It was a myth.
Which means the real tortures on this list... were often worse than the legends.
Number three.
The breaking wheel.
This one wasn't hidden in a dungeon.
It happened in the town square, in front of everyone.
Crowds came from miles away.
Some brought food.
Children watched from their parents' shoulders.
The condemned was tied to a large wooden wheel,
and the executioner struck his limbs, one by one, with a heavy iron bar.
Then the wheel was raised on a pole...
and left there, for the crows.
Sometimes, a merciful judge ordered one final blow first.
It was called the coup de grâce.
The blow of mercy.
Incredibly, the wheel was still used in Prussia in eighteen forty one.
But the wheel was justice, at least in their eyes.
Number two was pure cruelty.
Number two.
The brazen bull.
Two and a half thousand years ago, in Sicily,
the tyrant Phalaris wanted a new way to execute his enemies.
Phalaris was real.
He ruled the Greek city of Akragas, today called Agrigento.
A sculptor named Perillos built him a hollow bull, made of bronze.
A door on the side.
A fire underneath.
And inside the head, a system of tubes...
so the screams would come out as the sound of a bellowing bull.
According to legend, Phalaris was disgusted by the inventor,
and ordered him to test it himself.
Perillos became its first victim.
And the tyrant?
Years later, his own people rose up against him...
and it is said he died inside his own bull.
But number one... is worse.
Number one.
Scaphism.
It comes from ancient Persia, and it was described by the Greek writer, Plutarch.
The victim was placed between two boats, one on top of the other.
Only his head, hands and feet were left outside.
Then he was force fed milk and honey.
And more honey was poured over his face.
Then, he was left floating in a stagnant pond, under the burning sun.
And the insects came.
Every day, they fed him again.
Not out of mercy...
but to keep him alive.
According to Plutarch, a soldier named Mithridates survived like this...
for seventeen days.
And when the top boat was finally lifted...
there was almost nothing left of him.
Seven tortures.
Thousands of years.
And every one of them was invented by people who believed they were doing the right thing.
Which one do you think was the worst?
Tell me in the comments.
And if you want to know what it was like to survive one night in a medieval dungeon...
watch this next.
